ABSTRACT: We report a novel three-component radical
acylfluoroalkylation of 1,3-enynes by synergistic N-heterocyclic
carbene (NHC)/photoredox catalysis toward various fluorinated
allenic aryl ketones. This protocol features a broad substrate scope
and excellent functional group tolerability, with examples of late-
stage modification of drug molecules and natural products.
Notably, seven different fluoroalkyl motifs can be introduced to
1,3-enynes, further demonstrating the robustness and generality of
this method. The generation of the fluoroalkyl radical from each
sulfinate reagent was individually supported by EPR experiments.
F
luorine-containing molecules play a vital role in
pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals.
1
Consequently, the
development of efficient and selective fluorination and
perfluoroalkylation methods constitutes an important yet
highly challenging field in modern organic synthesis.
2
While
radical trifluoromethylation
3
has emerged as a powerful
strategy to introduce the CF
3
group, analogous difluorome-
thylation
4

5

less attention. This is quite surprising given that the CF
2
H and

2

known to serve as bioisosteric replacement of various
functional groups to improve therapeutic properties.
6
This
disconnect has been somewhat addressed, as shown by us
7
and
others
8
in a series of transformations involving styrene-type
substrates as radical acceptors. However, related processes
employing other kinds of unsaturated systems remain scarce.
In particular, fluoroalkylative 1,4-difunctionalization of 1,3-
enynes, despite recent advances,
9

installation of CF

Building on our previous work on styrenyl substrates,
10
we
asked if 1,3-enynes could be employed as potential coupling
partners toward acylfluoroalkylation (Scheme 1b). It is
noteworthy that, in addition to direct cross-coupling (A) and
Heck-type coupling (B), the current transformation may suffer
from other side pathways,
11
such as hydrofluoroalkylation (C)
and the formation of other regioisomers (D and E). Herein, we
report the successful development of a three-component
acylfluoroalkylation of 1,3-enynes via N-heterocyclic carbene
(NHC)/photoredox dual catalysis.
12

is universally applicable to an array of fluoroalkyl sulfinate
reagents without the need to reoptimize the reaction
conditions.

thiazolium (N2), oxazolium (N3), and imidazolylidenes (N4
and N5), were also examined, although no improvement in
yield was observed (entry 8). Further evaluation of the reaction

as the optimal base (entry 9−11)
and acetone as the superior solvent (see Table S4), while
changing the concentration, light source, and intensity did not
lead to higher yields (see Tables S5−7). Control experiments
demonstrated that the reaction did not occur in the absence of
catalyst, base, or light irradiation (Table S8).
With the optimized conditions in hand, we surveyed the
generality of this three-component coupling (Scheme 2). Thus,
electronically diverse 4-aryl-1,3-enynes bearing various func-
tional groups were found to be viable substrates to afford the
desired products 6−20 in moderate to good yields, including
useful synthetic handles such as halides (10 and 11) and
cyanide (14). In the case of a nitro substituent, we observed
exclusive 1,4-hydrodifluoromethylation (15), while a formyl
group shut down the reaction (18). Furthermore, heteroarenes
underwent a smooth reaction in good yields (21−22).
Notably, 4-alkyl-1,3-enynes could also be employed in this
transformation (23−24), albeit in diminished yields. Besides,
reactions using monosubstituted (25) and internal 1,3-enynes
(26) proceeded efficiently, thus offering variability in the
substitution pattern of the product allenes. Next, the scope of
acyl fluorides was evaluated. Electronic and steric perturbations
were generally tolerated (27−38). In particular, bromo- (29)
and even iodo-substituted (35) acyl fluorides furnished the
respective products in good yields. Though less efficient, a
benzofuran motif could also be incorporated (39). Excitingly,
we found that, in addition to acyl fluorides, dicarbonates and
acid anhydrides could also participate in the reaction toward
products containing an ester and an aliphatic ketone moiety,
respectively (40 and 41), thus representing a substantial
expansion of chemical space beyond (hetero)aryl substituents.

Similar to previous cases, no significant influence on the
reaction outcome was observed upon the modification of the
arene electronics. Thus, this method offers straightforward
access to various fluoroalkylated allenic compounds without
the need to adjust the reaction conditions to accommodate
different fluoroalkylating reagents.
Our protocol can be applied to the late-stage functionaliza-
tion of pharmaceutical or bioactive compounds. For instance,
acyl fluoride derived from mefenamic acid (67) as well as 1,3-
enyne derivatives of dihydroartemisinin (68), ibuprofen (69),
and estrone (70) were found to be efficient coupling partners.
Several experiments were conducted to gain some insight
into the mechanism (Scheme 3). In the radical trap
experiments, the addition of 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidinyloxy
(TEMPO) or diphenyl ethylene (DPE) to the standard
conditions effectively inhibited the acyldifluoromethylation
process. The formation of adducts 71−73 indicated the
presence of fluoroalkyl radicals in the process (Scheme 3a).

which then enters the NHC catalytic cycle upon reaction with

reduced by Ir(II) to generate ketyl radical F while closing the
photoredox cycle. Intermolecular radical−radical cross-cou-

fluoroalkylated allenyl ketone product 4 and regenerates N1′.
Alternatively, propargyl radical B can undergo coupling with F
to form 1,2-addition side product 5.
In summary, we have developed an efficient three-
component acylfluoroalkylation of 1,3-enynes via NHC/PC
cooperative catalysis. Various 1,3-enynes and acyl fluorides are
compatible, and a range of functional groups can be tolerated.
